component.name: EloraNotes
component.summary: A calm, minimalistic Markdown notes app

description.p: EloraNotes is a quiet, keyboard-friendly home for Markdown notes: folders, tags, wiki links and backlinks, a command palette, split editing with a live preview, and a soft glow highlight for the text that matters.

Pictures in shared notes now travel reliably. The frames that carry them were added without a protocol version bump, so a server from before picture sharing accepted the connection and dropped every picture without saying anything: the note’s text arrived for everyone, the picture only for the computer that added it. The protocol is now version 3, so an older server is refused at connect with a message to update it (and an older client is refused the same way) instead of losing the picture quietly.
Note cards in the sidebar can drop their preview line from Settings, leaving the title, date and tags on a shorter card, so more notes fit in the list at once.
The note list’s scroll bar now has a strip of its own along the right of the list, so it no longer floats over the note cards.

The shared library is headed by its cloud alone now, without a folder glyph in front of it, so it no longer reads as a folder on this computer. The library also keeps folders of its own: a shared note filed from its folder menu brings its folder to everyone’s sidebar, where it can be folded shut like any other.
The sidebar shows what belongs to what: a folder’s notes are stepped in from its header, and notes inside the shared library are stepped in further — twice over when they sit in one of its folders.

Pictures can now be put into a note without writing Markdown by hand: the new picture button in the formatting bar opens the file chooser, a picture dropped on the window joins the note, and a screenshot pasted with Ctrl+V lands at the caret. Pictures keep their proportions and are resized by dragging the square in their bottom-right corner in Preview or Split; the size is written into the note as {width=…} so it survives a restart. Each picture is copied into an attachments folder beside the notes and named after its contents, so the same picture is stored once and two people's screenshots never collide.

Pictures in a shared note are now stored on the server too, so everyone with the library sees them and they are still there after the computer that added them is gone. A picture added before a note is moved to the server goes with it, and Copy to this computer brings the pictures along. The server’s notes folder stays an ordinary EloraNotes library, pictures included.

A connection that cannot be made now gives up after a few seconds and says why in Settings (timeout, refused, unknown host) instead of staying on “Connecting…” for minutes, with a note about the port, the firewall and the router.

The app icon no longer sits on a white square in taskbars and window lists. The icons were rasterised from the tile artwork with the transparent background requested after the file had already been read, so the rounded corners were filled in with opaque white and every place that drew the icon showed the square around it. The icon set — PNGs, the Windows .ico, the macOS .icns and the pixels the window hands to the window manager — is generated again with a real transparent background.

Clicking a shared note no longer pushes it to the top of the list: opening a note handed its text around and the server counted that as an edit, so the date the list sorts by moved every time. Only a change to the text counts now. The note's scroll bar sits against the window's edge instead of floating inside the margin beside the text, the marks that show who else has a note open are brushes, and Settings → Shared library has a "Your name" field: leave it empty to use the account name on this computer, or type a name to have others see that, which reaches them without reconnecting. The server needs this one too, for the note list part.

A client that speaks a different protocol version is now told so. The refusal was written to the socket but the connection was closed before it was sent, so an app left behind by an update looked like a server that had gone away. This release is otherwise 0.9.11, and replaces it: shared notes no longer show each other's text, a note is not overwritten by a copy the window was still showing, and a shared note can be taken out of its folder again. Both the app and the server need it.

Shared notes no longer show each other's text. Every live text frame now says which note it belongs to, so a frame still on the way when another note is opened is dropped instead of being merged into the note now on screen — that was why a note you switched back to could come up as the one you had just left, and settle only after a few switches. A shared note also no longer pushes the copy the window happens to be showing before the server has sent that note's own text. Taking a shared note out of its folder works: a cleared folder used to reach the server as "leave it alone", so the note stayed filed. The app and the server both need this one; the older side reports a version mismatch.

A new note in the shared library is its own note again. The app kept one Yjs document for every note it opened, so the text of the note being looked at travelled into the next room: creating a note while another was open made the new note a copy of the old one, and switching notes carried the previous text with it. The document now belongs to the note, updates still in flight from the note just left are dropped, and the server only relays a caret to the people in that note instead of to every connection. The server has to be updated as well: the presence part is on its side.

Pictures written into a note the way GitHub writes them — ![alt](path) — are now drawn in Preview and Split mode, with paths resolved from the note's own folder. PNG, JPEG and GIF pictures load from disk, and http(s) links are downloaded in the background and cached, so a note can point at a screenshot next to it or at an image on the web. A shared note no longer reports "Auto-save error" when its text is formatted or it is pinned: those went to a file on disk that a note living on the server does not have. The name tag by somebody else's caret is now a filled chip, so the line above it no longer shows through the name, and it moves below the caret when there is no room above. The Edit tab and its command palette entry use the Tabler brush instead of a pencil, and the note column now fills a large or fullscreen window instead of stopping at a fixed width, which used to leave wide empty bands on either side.

People no longer linger on a shared note after they leave it. Closing a shared note, or switching to another one or to a personal note, tells the others straight away; a connection that goes away without saying goodbye — the app quit, or a machine that dropped off — is cleared out by the server with the presence update the other clients need to drop the name and caret. Opening a shared note also shows who is already editing it, instead of only the people who happen to move afterwards. Presence is now tracked per connection rather than by name, so two people who use the same account name no longer take each other's caret away when one of them leaves. The server has to be updated as well for the disconnects and the join-time list.

Shared notes now update as they are typed. The connection asks the window to draw the moment somebody else's keystroke arrives, instead of waiting for the next move of the local mouse or the caret's blink, so the other person's words appear letter by letter. The caret also belongs to the words around it: when somebody inserts a line above the text being edited, the caret and its selection travel down with that text rather than staying behind in what the other person just wrote, and if that pushes the line out of view the editor follows it.

The Windows server installer no longer stops with "The system cannot find the file specified" when it checks for an existing server: the scheduled-task lookup reads its result instead of treating a missing task as an error. It also asks, as the Linux installer does, whether to update an existing server, uninstall it and keep the notes, uninstall it and delete them, or cancel, and it stops the running server before replacing its binary so the copy cannot hit a file in use.

The folder menu on a note now lists the connected server under "Shared libraries": picking it moves the note into the shared library with its body, folder, tags, pin and icon, and the local file goes once the server has it. A shared note offers "Copy to this computer" instead. The server installer, run on a machine that already has a server, now asks whether to update it, uninstall it and keep the notes, uninstall it and delete them, or cancel.

With a shared note open, New (and the daily-note, template and wiki-link actions) now creates the note in the server's library instead of on your own disk: it joins the same folder, keeps the tag you are filtering by, and appears on everyone's sidebar straight away. The server writes it as an ordinary Markdown file with the folder, tags and body the client sent.

The server installer works on systems with a read-only /etc/systemd/system, such as NixOS: it registers a per-user service, keeps the notes in ~/.local/share/elora-server, turns on lingering so it still starts at boot, and prints the systemctl --user commands that manage it. A certificate from an earlier interrupted install is carried over with any notes, so the code clients confirm does not change.

The server installer creates the service group before the service user, so it no longer stops with "chown: invalid group" on systems where useradd does not make a group of its own, and an install left over from an earlier release is moved onto that group. The settings and key are readable only by the service user.

The server installer now downloads to a temporary folder before installing, so a read-only /usr/local or a full disk gets a clear message instead of a failed transfer, falls back to /opt/elora-server when /usr/local/bin cannot be written, and checks that the binary it installed actually runs. Settings are written without relying on sudo being present, and the network download reports the reason when it cannot complete.

Shared notes. One machine runs the EloraNotes server, which keeps the notes as plain Markdown files and serves them over TLS with a certificate each client pins on the first connection. Everyone who connects sees the server's notes in the sidebar under its name and edits them together: text merges as it is typed, each person's caret carries their name and colour, and a note somebody has open shows a dot on its card. Usernames come from the account each person is logged into, and the library structure (titles, folders, tags, pins, trash) travels with the text.

Installers for the server are included with this release for Linux and Windows; they ask for the server name, port and password, start it at boot and open the port in the firewall. The app gains a Shared library section in Settings.

The seam between the note list and the editor is a single soft divider now. It had been painted underneath the sidebar, so what showed there was the note list's scroll bar, drawn in the text colour; scroll bars rest faint and out of the way.

The divider beside the note list is softer and sits between even margins instead of leaving a wide empty band, and a window too narrow for two columns shows the editor alone rather than two cramped panes. The README screenshot shows the current look.

The Matugen theme works in the Flatpak: the sandbox now includes ~/.config/elora read-only, and the app looks for the generated colours there when its own config folder (the sandbox's private one) has none.

The Flatpak now includes the home Documents folder by name, because the XDG documents directory points at nothing on systems without a user-dirs file, which left the app with an empty, temporary home instead of the notes in Documents/EloraNotes.

The AppImage no longer carries its own copy of the Wayland client library: the graphics driver has to use the host's, so shipping one made the image fail to start on hosts whose driver expects a newer copy.

Installing a newer Flatpak bundle now replaces the copy the launcher runs, so the version installed is the version that starts, and the AppImage bundles the Wayland and keyboard libraries it needs instead of assuming the host provides them.
The Flatpak now updates itself like every other build, and Settings gained an Updates section that checks on demand and installs the result.
The colour controls in the formatting bar move as one group instead of splitting across rows at narrow widths, and closing the sidebar no longer leaves the note centred in a narrow column.
The sidebar's Notes, Pinned and Trash sections share one row again, with Trash reduced to its glyph.
Notes and settings now live in Documents/EloraNotes on every platform, which the Flatpak shares with other installs instead of keeping a private copy.
Packaging for every platform: AppImage, Flatpak, a Windows setup wizard, a macOS app bundle and portable builds, plus an in-app updater that understands each one.
